summary: An April 1 RFC and a humorous one. It is a parody of the Internet standards process, written as if documenting how a Roman community standardizes protocols, with stages, document types and even intellectual property rules. It is informational, not a real standards process.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st parody describes how a fictional Roman community would make technical standards. It mirrors formal standards procedures with Roman names and numerals.

subtitle: An April 1st parody of a standards process, recast for an imaginary Roman community.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke recasts a formal standards process as the work of a fictional Roman community.
tldr.mechanism: It describes mock standards bodies, publication types, maturity levels, review steps, appeals, and intellectual-property rules.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is satire written in the style of a process document, not an actual standards process.

today: RFC 2551 is an Informational April 1st parody. Its fictional Roman standards process is a joke, not an operating standards procedure.

sections.title: A Roman Standards Process
sections.content:
The memo presents a process for creating standards in an imagined “Roman” network community. It describes bodies called the Roman Architecture Board and Roman Engineering Steering Group, using Roman numerals throughout.

The document's table of contents and detailed procedures imitate a real standards-process specification. Its Roman framing makes the formal language part of the satire.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC pretends that a Roman network community has its own standards organization. It describes the process in a mock-formal style.

sections.title: Specifications and Maturity Levels
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes Technical Specifications, which describe protocols or formats, from Applicability Statements, which explain when and how specifications apply. It also defines “required,” “recommended,” and “elective” levels.

Its fictional standards track has Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Roman Standard stages. Other documents can be Experimental, Informational, or Historic, and a separate Worst Current Practice series records community guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The imaginary system has different document types and approval stages. A proposal gains maturity through review and experience.

sections.title: Review, Appeals, and Open Records
sections.content:
The memo describes public drafts, community review, Last-Call periods, approval by the RESG, and publication as RFCs. It also sets out advancement, revision, retirement, and appeals procedures.

Other sections cover using external specifications, keeping public records, allowing narrow variances, and handling intellectual-property rights. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Ideas are reviewed publicly before approval, and people can appeal decisions. The document also imagines rules for records, exceptions, and ownership rights.
